lessons.gloss: friend — a Persian word that literally means "the one you chose"

segments.text: Four things you can ask for — pāṇī, cāh, dudh, roṭī. This chapter turns from things to people, starting with the one Chapter 2's ਤੂੰ was really for.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: ਦੋਸਤ — dost — friend.
ਦ d, ੋ the o sign, ਸ s, ਤ t. Every letter already yours, from ਦੋ, "two," and ਸਤਿ, "truth."

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a friend is a chosen thing

segments.text: ਦੋਸਤ (dost) is Persian, not Sanskrit — borrowed from Classical Persian dōst, from Old Persian dauštā. Its root is Proto-Indo-European, meaning roughly "to taste, to choose." Latin took the taste sense and left English gusto and disgust, both through gustare. Germanic took the choosing sense and left Old English cēosan, modern English choose. Persian took a third path: the "chosen" one became the word for a friend.

So dost sits beside roṭī as this book's second honest gap: roṭī's own root is lost to time; dost's is not lost, but it belongs to Persian, not to the Sanskrit line most of your nouns so far have followed.

lessons.title: ਪਰਿਵਾਰ (parivār) — what surrounds you
lessons.gloss: family — literally "what surrounds you," built from two Sanskrit pieces you can pull apart

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: ਦੋਸਤ (dost) named one person, chosen. This word names the group you never chose at all.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: ਪਰਿਵਾਰ — parivār — family.
ਪ p, ਰ r, ਿ short i, ਵ v — the same ਵ you read in ਵੇਖਣਾ — ਾ long ā, ਰ r again. Pa-ri-vā-r, four syllables, no new letter in any of them.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — two Sanskrit pieces, still visible

segments.text: ਪਰਿਵਾਰ comes straight from Sanskrit parivāra, and unlike dost or roṭī, this one splits cleanly into two working pieces: pari-, "around," plus vṛ-, "to cover, to surround." A parivāra is, word for word, what encloses you — the same pari- that opens parikramā, a walk made around something sacred, and a vṛ- that also sits inside varṇa, "covering" — the word Sanskrit used for both colour and social class.
Unlike dost, this is Sanskrit through and through. Unlike roṭī, its root is not a mystery — you can point at both halves and say what each one meant on its own.

lessons.title: ਭਰਾ (bharā) — a breathy letter you have not met yet
lessons.gloss: brother — spelled with a breathy bh, said with a plain p and a low tone

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called The letters in this word and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Kòṛā the horse dipped and rose because its old ਘ lost its breath at the start of the word. This chapter's word does the same thing, with a different consonant, and it is not a verb this time — it is somebody you know.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: ਭਰਾ — bharā — brother.
ਭ — new: the fourth letter of the p-row, once bha, a b said with a breathy voice. Then ਰ r, ਾ long ā.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need — the other half of the tone rule

segments.text: Chapter 7 showed word-initial ਘ losing its breath and leaving a low, rising pitch — kòṛā. ਭ is the same story with a different letter: said at the front of a word, its breath is gone too, and what is left is a plain, voiceless p, plus a low tone on the vowel after it.
ਭਰਾ is therefore not said bharā. It is said prā̀ — p, not bh, and low on the first vowel. Spelling keeps the old consonant; speech keeps only its pitch.

utterances: position in the word: initial (bh-, gh- …) old sound: breathy voice. what survives: low tone, consonant plain.
position in the word: medial (-jh-, -ḍh- …) old sound: breathy voice. what survives: high, falling tone.
position in the word: final, nothing after. old sound: any lost breath. what survives: high, level tone.

segments.text: Three positions, three outcomes, and you have now met a word for each.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the cleanest cousin in this book

segments.text: bharā is inherited from Sanskrit bhrātṛ, root Indo-European bʰréh₂tēr. This is one of the cleanest cognate sets in the family: Sanskrit bhrātṛ, English brother, Latin frāter, Greek phrātēr, Russian brat — every one of them the same word, by ordinary sound change, in every branch, no borrowing anywhere. Where parivār kept both its Sanskrit halves intact, bharā shows what centuries of everyday wear does instead: the whole cluster bhr- thinned down to a single consonant and a tone.

lessons.title: ਭੈਣ (bhaiṇ) — the same tone, a different family tree
lessons.gloss: sister — the same low tone as brother, but not the same family of words

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say ਭਰਾ (bharā) the way it is actually said — prā̀, low. This chapter's last word starts with the same letter and the same tone. Whether it shares brother's family tree is a separate question.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: ਭੈਣ — bhaiṇ — sister.
Said pàiṇ — the same ਭ becomes p + low tone shift as ਭਰਾ (bharā), now on a different vowel, closed by the curled-back ਣ you already read in ਜਾਣਨਾ.

ਭ bh, already yours from bharā — the second word in this book to use it. ੈ the ai-sign, from ਹੈ. ਣ retroflex n. Three letters, none of them new, and the tone is the same rule as last lesson, run again.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a share, not a sibling-word

segments.text: ਭੈਣ (bhaiṇ) is inherited from Sanskrit bhaginī, built on bhaga-, "a share, a portion" — a sister, etymologically, as one who holds a share. That root is Indo-Aryan, not a straight PIE kinship term: the old Proto-Indo-European word for "sister," swésōr, is exactly what gives English sister — and Sanskrit simply stopped using it, replacing it with this one instead.

So ਭਰਾ (bharā) and ਭੈਣ (bhaiṇ) are not a matched pair the way English brother and sister feel like one. Bharā is the unbroken PIE cousin of brother. Bhaiṇ is a homegrown Indo-Aryan replacement, unrelated in root to sister — even though both now open with the identical bh-become-p-plus-low-tone sound, purely by coincidence of which consonant each word once started with.

segments.prompt: Is bhaiṇ the same word as English sister by unbroken descent, the way bharā is the same word as brother?

feedback.correct: Right: bhaiṇ comes from bhaginī, built on bhaga- 'a share' — Sanskrit replaced the old PIE sister-word, which survives in English sister instead.
feedback.incorrect: No. bhaiṇ descends from bhaginī, 'a share-holder,' not from the PIE word that gives English sister; only bharā is the unbroken cousin of its English counterpart.
